headline: OpenHands can write and modify shared runtime state while AutoGPT can read/write files and execute shell, creating medium-to-high risks of leakage, conflict, and unverified cascading actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can read and write filesystem content and execute shell; B can read/write runtime files and use MCP, so a shared workspace or mounted volume could carry attacker-controlled instructions between them. The pathway is plausible in default agent workflows, though not proven by the profiles alone. Uncertainty about the exact bridge escalates this above low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted directory or shared MCP resource, injected instructions can cross from one to the other.
IF either agent treats file contents as trusted prompts, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Disable MCP on the agent that does not need it.
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes files from the other.
Prefix all inter-agent files with provenance metadata.
requires-engineering: enforce content-type and provenance filtering on shared channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly touches files mounted into its runtime and has broad network egress; A can access the filesystem and shell. If sensitive files are mounted into the shared workspace, B can transmit them outward, while A can also expose local data through its own file access. The profiles do not prove sensitive data is present, so this stays medium rather than high.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into B's runtime, B can read and exfiltrate them over broad egress.
IF A and B share a filesystem, either agent can surface the other's local artifacts in outputs.
mitigations: Mount only minimal, non-sensitive files.
Use separate per-agent directories.
Turn off network egress for the agent handling sensitive files.
Rotate or redact secrets before mounting workspaces.
requires-engineering: add DLP or egress allowlisting at the runtime boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can execute shell and spawn subprocesses; B can write the filesystem, modify git state, install packages, and also execute shell. In a shared directory, both can mutate the same repo or runtime state without any locking mechanism being stated, so concurrent writes and git corruption are plausible in default use. This matches the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted volume, they can overwrite each other's changes.
IF either agent runs package installs or git operations concurrently, state corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Serialize write operations with a lock file.
Disable git writes for one agent.
Snapshot the workspace before each run.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B has browser, shell, and filesystem actions, so if it consumes A's outputs as authoritative, A's mistakes can become real actions. A can generate content from shell/file access, and B can then act on it without a verification step being documented. That creates a default pathway from generated text to irreversible side effects, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF B uses A's output as task instructions without independent verification, errors cascade into actions.
IF A produces file-derived claims that B then executes in browser or shell, downstream harm can occur.
mitigations: Require B to verify A's claims against source files.
Insert a human approval gate before any action-taking step.
Limit B to read-only mode for planning tasks.
Log and diff all proposed actions before execution.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles files mounted into its runtime and model provider API keys, while A has filesystem access and network egress. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so a compliance mismatch cannot be proven; however, the shared file-handling and outbound connectivity create a plausible retention/residency mismatch if regulated data is mounted. Uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into B's runtime, its handling and retention must match the governing policy.
IF A or B logs file contents to external services, residency or retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Do not mount regulated data into either agent.
Review retention settings before enabling runs.
Use region-appropriate model endpoints.
Redact identifiers from files before processing.
requires-engineering: document and enforce data-processing agreements and residency controls.
